extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; practicing journalists interested in professional ideals
extracted.subtask_description: Historical/practical standards and professional criteria for newspaper editors and editorial writing: personal qualities, ethical duties, institutional responsibilities, audience strategies, and procedural guidance for investigative/editorial work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor must be able to write and judge writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "The great editor is by no means the great writer, but he ought to be able to write and must be a judge of writing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that an editor should have active writing competence and critical judgment of prose; this is presented as a basic professional requirement of the editor's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive knowledge of newspaper operations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The newspaper office is a little kingdom. The able editor needs to know and does know every range of it between the editorial room, the composing room and the pressroom."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An editor should understand all departments and functions, having 'risen... step by step from the ground floor to the roof.' Practical managerial familiarity with production processes is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced temperament and critical faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: "He should be level-headed yet impressionable; sympathetic yet self-possessed; able quickly to sift, detect and discriminate; of varied knowledge, experience and interest... Nothing too small for him to tackle, nothing too great, he should keep to the middle of the road..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor's personal qualities include emotional balance, sympathy combined with self-possession, rapid critical discernment, breadth of knowledge, and the willingness to address matters of all scales while avoiding extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness and rejection of personal gain
rubrics_metrics.description: "Disinterestedness being the soul of successful journalism, unselfish devotion to the noble purpose in public and private life... seeking never anything further for himself. ... he should say to preferment as to bribery, 'Get behind me, Satan.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical injunction that editors must be motivated by public service rather than personal advancement or bribery; independence from financial or political temptations is presented as central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, answerability, and trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: "This public insists upon some visible presence. ... personal journalism cannot be escaped ... it must be clear and answerable, responsive to the common weal, and, above all, trustworthy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers (and the people of power behind them) must be visible and publicly accountable; legal requirements in some states reinforce the need for identifiable, answerable leadership to maintain public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper as teacher and moral influence
rubrics_metrics.description: "As the world passes ... the daily journal is destined, if it survives as a power, to become the teacher — the very Bible of the people. The people are already beginning to distinguish between the wholesome and the meretricious in their newspapers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press is cast as a civic educator; editors and owners should aim for wholesome content and character to fulfill the paper's pedagogical and moral role in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation correlates with influence and party affiliation pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: "The paper with the largest circulation was necessarily the most influential, and the larger circulation generally meant affiliation with the dominant party."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical historical observation that reach brings political influence and that commercial pressures and political alignment often accompany attempts to maximize circulation—an institutional constraint editors must navigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-circulation papers as a check of idealism
rubrics_metrics.description: "These facts, together with the increased cost of manufacturing a newspaper, would tend toward a purely commercial morality, were it not for the check that lies in the newspaper of small circulation but stiff idealism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local or smaller papers can serve as counterweights to commercialized, partisan mass papers by preserving reformist ideals and civic responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial mission to civic reform and the common good
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Star was dedicated ... to honest elections, to democratic government, to the abolition of special privilege, to fair dealings on the part of public service corporations, to larger opportunities ... to progress toward social and industrial justice..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model presented (Kansas City Star) frames the newspaper's purpose as active trusteeship for civic betterment—advocacy for honest elections, fair government and social progress is an explicit editorial criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence, detachment from party, and seriousness of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "His finished criticism... his complete detachment from party, helped to form a new school of journalists, as the example he set of a serious and lofty conception of an editor's duties helped to add dignity to the position."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises editors who adopt detached, non-partisan criticism and a serious conception of duty; such independence is framed as formative for professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage to oppose popular opinion and denounce demagoguery
rubrics_metrics.description: "To him, the less popular a view was, so much the more did it need to be well weighed, and if approved, to be strenuously and incessantly preached. Democracies will always have demagogues... What they need is men who will swim against the stream... Such a one was Edwin Godkin."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are urged to speak uncomfortable truths, resist populist pressures, and persist in arguments judged right even if unpopular—civic courage is an evaluative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness, factual accuracy, and willingness to correct errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The text criticizes Godkin for never making "a retraction or rectification of personal charges shown to be incorrect," and notes that this undermines fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard that good journalism/editorial practice includes fair treatment of opponents and readiness to retract or correct factual mistakes; failure to do so is identified as a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulitzer's procedural standards for editorial investigation and exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: "I want you to go into the Maynard case with an absolutely unprejudiced mind. ... I want you to get together all the documents in the case. I want you to take them home and study them as minutely as if you were preparing yourself for an examination. I want you to regard yourself as a judicial officer, oath-bound to justice, and when you shall have mastered the facts and the law in the case, I want you to set them forth in a four column editorial that every reader of the World can easily understand."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete procedural rubric: approach issues without prejudice; collect and study all documents thoroughly; adopt the mindset of a judicial officer bound to justice; present facts and law clearly and accessibly to ordinary readers. These are presented as 'praecepta of journalism.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-oriented accessibility and presentation techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: "It was the discovery that in New York... there was a large uneducated or semi-educated population who were not reading newspapers... The Pulitzer journalism ... addressed itself ... to those less fortunately conditioned. ... large type and black headlines... the same appeal for the patronage of the uneducated..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial and design choices (clear language, larger type, bold headlines, targeted subject matter) should be tailored to reach semi-educated or previously unserved readerships; accessibility is treated as a legitimate strategic and ethical aim.
